edges.description: A mild microtubule-stability deficit is nonetheless sufficient to derail cerebellar development, the tissue this disorder identifies as most sensitive.
The motor phenotype that names the syndrome, arising on a background of severe cerebellar hypoplasia.

nodes.description: The tissue-level lesion, and the disorder's central biological claim. All three affected individuals showed severe cerebellar hypoplasia, while the basal ganglia - malformed in the dominant TUBB2B disorder - were spared. The authors draw the general inference: this case reinforces the sensitivity of the developing cerebellum to microtubule defects. Whatever sets the threshold for microtubule dysfunction, the cerebellum crosses it first.

nodes.description: The molecular lesion, and the reason this disease is recessive. R390Q is a functionally mild allele: it does not affect the ability of beta-tubulin to fold, to be assembled into the alpha/beta heterodimer, or to be incorporated into microtubule polymers - the three failure modes that make other TUBB2B alleles dominant. What it does produce, modelled in the yeast TUB2 orthologue, is normal growth under basal conditions with increased sensitivity to microtubule-depolymerizing drugs. An allele that only reveals itself under challenge is an allele that a single wild-type copy can compensate for, which is precisely what recessive inheritance means here.

genetic_context.description: Homozygous missense. PARTIAL_LOSS_OF_FUNCTION is the value the evidence supports and is deliberately different from the values used elsewhere in the tubulin family: this allele is NOT dominant-negative, because a dominant-negative subunit must incorporate into the polymer and this one incorporates normally without disabling it; and it is not a complete loss of function, because folding, dimerization and incorporation are all intact and basal function is preserved. The measured deficit is reduced resilience - increased sensitivity to depolymerization.

nodes.description: Habitual quadrupedal gait, the identifying feature of the syndrome and the reason it is also known as recessive quadrupedalism. It occurs on a background of severe cerebellar hypoplasia; the term is descriptive of the gait, not an explanation of it.
